question: What is the primary characteristic of a malignant neoplasm compared to a benign one?

options.A: It invades nearby tissues and spreads to other parts of the body.
options.B: It stops growing entirely after a few weeks without treatment.
options.C: It only affects older adults and ignores younger populations.
options.D: It stays localized in one spot and never grows very large.

explanation: Malignant neoplasms are cancerous because they can break away, invade surrounding structures, and travel through the blood or lymph system. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T12#GNS321_U1_T12_h1)

question: Why is prevention so important in cancer care?

options.A: It replaces the need for surgical removal of tumors in every single patient.
options.B: It completely eliminates the requirement for diagnostic lab testing.
options.C: It stops the disease early, reducing suffering and healthcare costs.
options.D: It guarantees that patients will never experience any genetic mutations in their lifetime.

explanation: Preventing cancer or catching it early spares your future patients from aggressive treatments and helps them live longer, healthier lives. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T12#GNS321_U1_T12_h1)

question: What is the main goal of primary prevention?

options.A: Rehabilitating a patient after major cancer surgery
options.B: Catching an existing disease during its very early stages
options.C: Providing palliative comfort during end-of-life care
options.D: Preventing a disease from ever occurring in a healthy person

explanation: Think of primary prevention as stopping trouble before it even starts—like protecting healthy people by reducing risk factors. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T12#GNS321_U1_T12_h2)

question: Which nursing intervention is the best example of primary cancer prevention?

options.A: Teaching a patient how to care for a surgical wound after tumor removal
options.B: Helping a newly diagnosed patient manage chemotherapy side effects
options.C: Administering the HPV vaccine to a group of adolescent students
options.D: Scheduling a routine screening mammogram for a 50-year-old woman

explanation: Giving the HPV vaccine prevents a viral infection that can lead to cervical cancer, fitting the definition of primary prevention. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T12#GNS321_U1_T12_h2)

question: What is the main purpose of secondary prevention, like routine screenings?

options.A: Stopping environmental toxins from entering the local community
options.B: Preventing healthy individuals from ever encountering risk factors
options.C: Restoring full physical strength after cancer treatment finishes
options.D: Detecting disease early when it is easiest and most successful to treat

explanation: Secondary prevention is all about catching things early through screening so you can tackle them before they grow into a bigger problem. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T12#GNS321_U1_T12_h3)

question: Why is a colonoscopy considered a secondary prevention tool?

options.A: It completely cures advanced metastatic tumors in the large intestine.
options.B: It boosts the patient's immune system to fight off new infections.
options.C: It prevents a person from ever eating foods that cause inflammation.
options.D: It finds and removes abnormal growths before they develop into full cancer.

explanation: Screenings like colonoscopies let us spot small polyps and take them out early, stopping cancer in its tracks! [learn more](GNS321_U1_T12#GNS321_U1_T12_h3)

question: When does tertiary prevention happen along the care continuum?

options.A: After a diagnosis and treatment have already occurred
options.B: While administering vaccines in a community health clinic
options.C: During routine screening tests for healthy people
options.D: Before any exposure to environmental toxins happens

explanation: Tertiary prevention steps in after treatment to help patients recover, manage long-term effects, and get back to daily life. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T12#GNS321_U1_T12_h4)

question: Which nursing action best demonstrates tertiary cancer prevention?

options.A: Encouraging a young adult to stop smoking cigarettes before any disease develops
options.B: Teaching arm exercises to a patient recovering from breast cancer surgery to prevent lymphedema
options.C: Providing educational pamphlets about the importance of getting a regular Pap smear
options.D: Administering a routine hepatitis B immunization to a healthcare worker

explanation: Managing complications and rehabilitating a patient post-treatment are core goals of tertiary prevention. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T12#GNS321_U1_T12_h4)

question: When should a nurse refer a patient for genetic counseling regarding cancer?

options.A: The patient has a strong family history suggesting an inherited gene mutation.
options.B: The patient needs immediate chemotherapy for an active lung tumor.
options.C: The patient wants to quit smoking and needs nicotine replacement therapy.
options.D: The patient requires physical therapy to recover from radiation fatigue.

explanation: If a family history points to inherited genes, genetic counseling helps patients understand their risks and plan ahead. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T12#GNS321_U1_T12_h5)

question: Which of these is NOT a role for a nurse doing community cancer advocacy?

options.A: Prescribing targeted chemotherapy drugs for newly diagnosed patients
options.B: Promoting clean air and smoke-free public spaces
options.C: Dispelling cultural myths about cancer transmission in local neighborhoods
options.D: Advocating for policies that provide affordable cancer screenings

explanation: Nurses rock at education and community advocacy, but prescribing medications is reserved for doctors and specialized nurse practitioners. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T12#GNS321_U1_T12_h5)
